hero_badge: Open source · Built on RustDesk · AGPL-3.0
hero_subtitle: Remote desktop for your Mac from Windows, iPad or another Mac, built on the open-source RustDesk engine. Direct connection on your LAN or Tailscale, no accounts, no cloud. The Mac's displays, as they are, in one window or several.
hero_caption: Two displays of one Mac, each in its own window — or all of them at once.
features_title: Everything a remote desktop should do, without the account
features_desc: Direct, discovered, notarized and open source. The Mac's monitors stay the Mac's business.
feat_fit_desc: Pick which of the Mac's displays you see, open each one in its own window, or show them all at once on the desktop clients.
feat_dyn_desc: Want a monitor the size of your window? Add a virtual display on the Mac with SimpleDisplay (free, open source) or macOS itself. Remote Display shows it like any other display and never changes your Mac's configuration.
feat_scale_title: Finds your Mac, at home and away
feat_scale_desc: Computers on your LAN show up by themselves, and the Mac tells clients its Tailscale address, so it stays reachable from other networks. Pick the network per computer; passwords are remembered per address.
feat_profile_desc: On an iPad, put one of the Mac's displays on the connected monitor and keep another one on the iPad, with trackpad-style touch input.
feat_multi_desc: The server and the Mac client are signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple. Everything is AGPL-3.0 on GitHub, built on RustDesk 1.4.9.
feat_private_desc: Direct connection on your LAN or VPN with a password you set. No accounts, no IDs, no third-party servers. Everything is open source.
why_title_1: Remote desktops want an account, an ID
why_title_2: and a relay in the middle.
why_desc: Remote Display started as a fork of RustDesk to control a Mac Studio from a Windows PC over Tailscale without signing up anywhere: a direct connection with a password, machines discovered on the LAN, and the same Mac reachable from outside. It shows the Mac's displays as they are; the monitors themselves are configured on the Mac — with SimpleDisplay if you want virtual ones.
why_before_desc: An account, a device ID and a relay server between you and your own Mac.
why_after_desc: Your Mac, its password, your network. Nothing else in between.
how_title_2: a Mac-first server and clients on top
how_desc: Remote Display is a fork of RustDesk 1.4.9. The engine, the protocol and the client plumbing are RustDesk's; the serverless discovery, the Tailscale-aware clients, the macOS menu-bar server and the stability work for mirrored displays are what this project adds.
how_rustdesk_desc: Screen capture, video encoding, input injection and the encrypted direct connection all come from the RustDesk engine, vendored with its changes documented in the repository. Remote Display would not exist without it.
how_server_desc: A menu-bar app bundling the engine as a per-user service. It shows the Mac's displays as macOS reports them — physical ones and any virtual display you add with SimpleDisplay — and ignores the reconfiguration noise a hardware mirror produces, so a mirrored display no longer restarts the video every second.
how_client_desc: A Flutter app on top of the same engine: known computers with their addresses and which of them answer from where you are, one password per address, and a display menu with open-in-new-window and all displays.
how_transport_desc: RustDesk's protocol over a direct IP connection, no rendezvous or relay. LAN peers are discovered automatically, and the server announces its Tailscale address so clients reach it from other networks through your own VPN.
how_measured_desc: macOS 26 has quirks around display reconfiguration (mirror sets, per-process display lists, capture streams that go silent). The repository keeps the harnesses and VM notes that measured them.
start_desc: A server on the Mac, a client wherever you are.
start_server_desc: Install Remote Display Server from the DMG, turn the service on, grant Screen Recording and Accessibility, and set a password. It lives in the menu bar. Want a virtual monitor? Add it with SimpleDisplay; it shows up as one more display.
start_first_launch_desc: The DMGs are signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so macOS opens them without warnings. The server then asks once for Screen Recording and Accessibility in System Settings → Privacy & Security.
start_step2: Step 2 · on your PC, tablet or phone
start_client_desc: Connect to the Mac's IP on port 21118 with that password, or tap it in Your computers. Then open the display menu in the toolbar: pick a display, open it in a new window, or show all of them.
dl_desc: Every build is published on GitHub Releases. Install the server on the Mac you want to reach, then a client on each device you connect from.
dl_host_tag: Host · Apple silicon Mac · macOS 14 or newer
dl_host_desc: A menu-bar app for the Mac you connect to. Signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple.
dl_win_desc: Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit. Installer or portable zip.
dl_ios_desc: Development-signed IPA: install with Xcode or a sideloading tool.
lim_desc: Remote Display talks directly to your Mac. Here's what that means in practice.
lim_1: Remote Display does not create virtual monitors or change the Mac's display configuration: use SimpleDisplay or macOS for that; the client shows whatever displays the Mac has.
lim_2: "All displays" is available on the desktop clients (Windows, macOS); the iPad shows one display at a time, plus one on an external monitor.
lim_3: No relay yet: connections are direct, on your LAN or through a VPN.
lim_4: macOS builds are Apple silicon only for now. The server and the Mac client are notarized; the iOS build uses development signing.
community_desc: Remote Display is free software built on RustDesk: the engine inside is a modified copy of RustDesk 1.4.9 (AGPL-3.0), and the idea of a display that becomes the window comes from Tart.
